set.overview: A long, tiring day on the Holy Cross Wilderness trail system that ends with a ridge traverse. The route climbs the north ridge of Mount of the Holy Cross over boulders, then follows the connecting ridge southwest to the small rocky summit of Holy Cross Ridge. Everything is Class 2, but the talus is relentless and the mileage is high.
set.approach: Drive south from Minturn on the highway to the Tigiwon Road, about 8.5 miles of switchbacking gravel, and park at the Half Moon trailhead near 10,340 feet. Take the Holy Cross trail, not the Fall Creek trail, up about 1.7 miles to Half Moon Pass. Continue west roughly 1.4 miles down to East Cross Creek, cross it, and turn south onto the north ridge, where the path dissolves into boulders. The climbing proper begins at the creek.
set.descent_text: From the Holy Cross Ridge summit, retrace the connecting ridge back toward the saddle near 13,500 feet and pick the easiest line through the boulders. Most parties then go back down the north ridge to East Cross Creek and climb out to Half Moon Pass, or cross over the Holy Cross summit on the way. Reverse the approach trail to the trailhead from there.
hazards: Long stretches of large unstable boulders on the north ridge and the connecting ridge slow travel and risk twisted ankles
Afternoon lightning storms on the exposed, treeless ridge crest
Early-season snow on the north ridge may call for an ice axe
Very long day with a climb back up to Half Moon Pass at the end

evidence.fact: 13 mi round trip, about 5,835 ft gain from Half Moon trailhead
13 mi round trip; halved to 6.5 mi one way = 10.46 km

review.notes: Single source. Descent is retrace only (page gives no separate descent). Season skipped: no stated window. Page's 13 mi figure is consistent with its leg distances (1.7+1.4+2.6 to Holy Cross then ridge) so treated as the Holy Cross Ridge trip.

set.overview: The south face of Hagerman Peak is a steep talus and boulder climb through shallow couloirs and rock ribs above Geneva Lake in the Elk Mountains. It is mostly Class 2 with some Class 2+ moves on loose rubble, and snow can fill the gullies well into summer. The finish is a short walk west along the summit ridge.
set.approach: Reach the Geneva Lake trailhead in Lead King Basin near 9,685 feet by high-clearance four-wheel-drive road from Marble, taking the left fork at the Lost Trail Creek junction. Hike north and then west up switchbacks to Geneva Lake, passing the outlet on a log jam or the west shore trail, and wade or hop the feeder stream north of the lake. The trail climbs southeast to about 11,400 feet. Leave it at a stream crossing near 11,480 feet and follow the drainage north to the basin at 12,200 feet, where the gullies begin.
set.descent_text: Come down the same gullies and rubble you climbed, then follow the drainage back to the trail. If the couloirs still hold firm snow, an ice axe glissade can drop a thousand feet quickly. Walk the trail back past Geneva Lake to the trailhead.
hazards: Large loose talus and rubble in the gullies, with rockfall from other parties
Snow-filled couloirs early in the season that need an ice axe
Rough four-wheel-drive road with possible drifts and stream crossings
Feeder stream and outlet crossing at Geneva Lake in high water

evidence.fact: 9.7 mi round trip, about 4,155 ft from Geneva Lake trailhead
9.7 mi round trip; one way 4.85 mi = 7.80 km

review.notes: Single source. Season skipped (no window stated). Grade on page is 2+; row says Difficult Class 2.

set.overview: A straightforward off-trail tundra hike up the east side of Mount Oklahoma from the Halfmoon Creek valley south of Leadville. The route follows the North Halfmoon trail, then crosses willows and an open bench before a steep, loose tundra pitch to the east ridge and an easy walk to the summit. There is no exposure and routefinding is mild.
set.approach: Drive FR 110 west of Leadville past the Halfmoon campgrounds to the North Halfmoon Creek trailhead near 10,560 feet; high clearance is advised for the last half mile or so. Walk the old roadbed north, which becomes trail and gains only about 600 feet in two miles, and skip the branch to Mount Massive. Follow the North Halfmoon trail to just under 12,000 feet, then leave it and head west-southwest across the bench and a stream. The climbing begins where you turn north up the east ridge near 12,650 feet.
set.descent_text: Return by the same line: down the tundra ridge to the basin, east-northeast through the willows to the bench, and back to the North Halfmoon trail. Early in the season, firm snowfields on the slope can be glissaded with an ice axe.
hazards: Loose pebbly tundra on the steep east ridge pitch
Willow thrash and stream crossings below the basin
Early-season snowfields that call for an ice axe
Afternoon lightning on the open, treeless slopes

evidence.fact: about 8 mi round trip, about 3,300 ft gain
about 8 mi round trip; 4 mi one way = 6.44 km

review.notes: Single source; season skipped. Route on page is east ridge via North Halfmoon, matched to row's 'Southeast Slopes' above Halfmoon Creek.

set.overview: Jupiter Mountain is a remote Chicago Basin thirteener in the Weminuche, reached only by train or a very long backpack. The southwest slope is a steep Class 2+ climb over tundra, then loose talus to a west ridge and a false summit, with the true summit among rock towers that need a little routefinding and scrambling. Most parties camp in the basin and climb it with neighbouring peaks.
set.approach: Ride the narrow gauge train to Needleton Bridge at 8,235 feet, or backpack in from the highway. Cross to the east side of the Animas River, walk south about 0.8 miles to the signed junction, and turn left along Needle Creek. Follow it about 6 miles to Chicago Basin near 11,000 feet. Take either Columbine Pass trail to a meadow near 11,680 feet, then a faint climbers' path east-northeast across tundra to the base of the steep southwest slope.
set.descent_text: Come down the way you went up: the climbers' path off the slope to the 11,680-foot meadow, then the Columbine Pass trail back to Chicago Basin. Retrace the Needle Creek trail and the Animas River trail to Needleton and the train.
hazards: Loose talus and rubble on the steep upper slopes
Monsoon thunderstorms that make the climb unsafe on summer afternoons
Routefinding and minor scrambling among the towers near the false summit
High water at the Animas River crossing early in the season
Heavy crowding and a campfire ban in Chicago Basin in summer

evidence.fact: about 17 mi round trip, 5,630 ft total from Needleton (2,800 to camp + 2,830 above)
about 17 mi round trip; 8.5 mi one way = 13.68 km

review.notes: Single source. Season skipped (page gives only crowding and ford timing, no window). Train boarding rules changed in 2021; approach says 'or backpack' to stay safe.

set.overview: Turret Peak is a Chicago Basin thirteener climbed by its west-facing northwest slope, a plain Class 2 grind over talus, boulders and tundra. The slope is reached from the Pigeon-Turret saddle after a long approach from Needleton, and the summit itself takes about an hour round trip from the saddle. It is usually done together with Pigeon Peak.
set.approach: Ride the narrow gauge train to Needleton Bridge at 8,235 feet; there is no road. Follow the Ruby Creek route, steep with willows and a Class 2 bushwhack, up to the northwest Pigeon basin near 11,740 feet. Climb talus to the pass on Pigeon's south ridge at roughly 12,750 feet, then reach the Pigeon-Turret saddle. The climbing proper starts from the saddle on the slopes leading east to the summit.
set.descent_text: Go back down the west-facing slopes, staying north on the way down where the scree is easier, to the Pigeon-Turret saddle. From there descend the loose talus to the Ruby Creek camp or return over the saddle pass to the basin, and hike out to Needleton.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the descent from the saddle
Snow on the approach and near the saddle early in the season, so an ice axe helps
Marmots at the Ruby Creek camp chew into packs and tents
Monsoon rain that disrupts the train and raises the river
Wrong couloir between Turret and Peak Fifteen is technical fourth to fifth class

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: page gives only split approach figures that include Pigeon and camp-to-camp legs, no clean one-way trailhead-to-summit number. Season skipped.

set.overview: A long Class 2 day in the Sangre de Cristo Range that follows the Mount Lindsey trail to an open tundra basin and then heads north along a ridge to Huerfano Peak. The upper route is tundra turning to rubble and talus, with an optional scramble over the Iron Nipple. Exposure is minimal.
set.approach: Take the long gravel road from Gardner west on the Mosca Pass road and then the forest road to the Lily Lake trailhead near 10,725 feet; high clearance is recommended and road conditions should be checked first. Walk through forest and a big meadow, bypass the Lily Lake turnoff, and wade the Huerfano River. Climb steeply on the Lindsey trail to the tundra basin, aim for the saddle between Lindsey and the Iron Nipple, and turn north there on a fainter path.
set.descent_text: Return along the ridge and down the tundra and trail to the basin, then the Lindsey trail to the Huerfano River crossing and the trailhead. Strong parties sometimes continue north over two other points with some third-class scrambling, but the simple way down is the way up.
hazards: Huerfano River crossing without a bridge, more dangerous in runoff
Loose rubble, talus and scree on the upper ridge
Third-class moves on the Iron Nipple, avoidable by traversing below it
Remote access road that has closed after landslides
Afternoon thunderstorms above treeline

evidence.fact: 9.2 mi round trip, about 3,130 ft gain
9.2 mi round trip; 4.6 mi one way = 7.40 km

review.notes: Single source; page calls the line SW Ridge, row calls it South Slopes (description mentions Iron Nipple so same line). Season skipped.

set.overview: Rio Grande Pyramid is a remote Weminuche Wilderness summit reached by a long trail approach and a final stretch of tundra and loose volcanic boulders. The standard plan is an overnight from Thirtymile, camping near Weminuche Pass. Terrain is Class 2 and the routefinding is easy, but the trail fades on the upper slopes.
set.approach: Drive the graded dirt road from the highway west of Creede to Thirtymile Campground near 9,330 feet; a passenger car can make it. Start on Trail 818 and hike about 4.75 miles up to Weminuche Pass at 10,650 feet, crossing a footbridge about two miles in. From the pass take the faint trail west that contours around the east flank of the peak, or follow the Continental Divide Trail south and go west from there. Near 12,200 feet a spur leads to a saddle at about 12,645 feet, where the climbing starts.
set.descent_text: Retrace the route from the summit boulders back to the 12,645-foot saddle, where you can add the nearby thirteeners or descend directly. Follow the contouring trail to Weminuche Pass and the camp, then walk Trail 818 down to Thirtymile Campground.
hazards: Loose volcanic boulders on the final summit pile
Trail disappears on the tundra and rock above the saddle
Bridgeless La Vaca Creek crossing requires wading
Beetle-killed trees fall across trails in the forest
Bears around the Weminuche Pass camps, so store food carefully

evidence.fact: 19.7 mi round trip, 4,725 ft gain from Thirtymile Campground
19.7 mi round trip; 9.85 mi one way = 15.85 km

review.notes: Single source; the page's own approach table is internally inconsistent for the pass leg but the total RT figure is plausible (gain >= 13,825-9,330). Season skipped. Row calls the route East Slope/Ridge; page route comes up the east flank to the northeast ridge saddle.
